content.text:
We've now walked through not just the main flows but the awkward edges — empty screens, unreadable pages, non-links, very long entries, big piles, ordering, and remembering your preferences. I think we've reached a complete, coherent picture. Let me summarize where we've landed.

**So far, these behaviours are settled and confirmed by you:**

1. **Effortless saving** — paste a link, the page's details (title, description, site, icon, image) are pulled in, and you confirm a ready-made preview in one press.
2. **Fixing details** — correct the title or description in that same screen, either while saving or later via a clear **Edit** button.
3. **No accidental duplicates** — pasting a link you already have takes you straight to the existing one to update, never a second copy.
4. **Your own tags and notes** — reusable tags to keep things consistent, and notes with real formatting (headings, bold, lists, links).
5. **Reliable finding** — a search box with `#tags`, exact phrases, and `AND`/`OR`/`NOT`, plus click-a-tag filtering — all narrowing together, with friendly "nothing found" messages.
6. **To-read vs finished** — move links between the two without deleting, with All / To read / Finished views.
7. **Order and memory** — sort by newest, oldest, or title, and the app remembers your choice, manageable in **Settings**.
8. **Graceful edges** — welcoming empty states, non-links politely refused, unreadable pages still saveable, and long content that never breaks the layout.

A few things I've noted as **build-time matters** (not decisions for you now): making it fast with thousands of bookmarks, keeping everything saved to your personal account across devices, and fetching page details from the live web.

Everything so far has been an exploratory prototype — **not** the real application. My next phase would be to actually build this scope as the working app.

**May I start implementing this scope?**

content:
Not quite yet. The summary captures what we’ve explored, but there are several important parts of managing a growing collection that we haven’t settled:

- Opening a bookmark should take me to the original page. I also need to edit its address, not only its title and description, and permanently delete it when appropriate.
- I need a separate Archive. Archiving should hide a bookmark from the normal collection and search without deleting it, with an Archived view where I can restore it. This is separate from whether I’ve finished reading it.
- For larger cleanups, I need to select several bookmarks—or everything matching the current search or filters—and add or remove tags, change read status, archive, or delete them together.
- I’d like to save a useful combination of search text and included or excluded tags, so I can return to that same filtered view later.
- I want a preserved copy of a page in case the original changes or disappears, as well as an option to save it through the Internet Archive. For a PDF link, the preserved copy should be the PDF itself.
- I need to bring in my existing browser bookmarks and export the collection again without losing titles, tags, or saved dates.
- Settings should also cover how many items are shown and the text size, not just sorting.

Once we’ve worked through those behaviours and included them in the agreed scope, I’ll be comfortable approving implementation.

content.text:
The per-bookmark actions work. Open the two layouts below — they're identical except how a bookmark's actions are arranged. In **each**, try these three things:

1. **Open the original page** — click a bookmark's **title** (or its image). It opens the real page in a new browser tab.
2. **Edit its address** — press **Edit**; you'll see a new **"Address (link)"** field alongside title and description. Change it and Save — the bookmark now points to the new address.
3. **Delete it** — a confirmation appears (*"Delete permanently? This can't be undone."*); Cancel keeps it, Delete removes it for good.

The layouts differ in how actions are presented:

- **Option A — everything as buttons:** http://maker:4001/action-a.html
  *Edit*, the read-status toggle, and *Delete* are all visible on each card.

- **Option B — Edit shown, the rest under "More":** http://maker:4001/action-b.html
  *Edit* stays on the card; the status change and *Delete* live under a **More ▾** menu.

Why the layout matters: you've also asked for **Archive** and **bulk actions** next, so the number of per-bookmark actions is going to grow — Option B keeps cards tidy as that happens, Option A keeps everything one click away.

A couple of assumptions to check: opening always uses a **new tab**; **Delete is permanent and always asks first**; and editing the address **doesn't silently re-fetch** the page details (you stay in control of them).

**Which action layout do you prefer — and do opening, editing the address, and deleting all behave as you'd want?**

Opening: clicking a bookmark's title or its image opens the original page in a
new browser tab.

Per-bookmark action layout: Edit and the read-status toggle (Mark as finished /
Move to To-read) are shown directly on each card because they are used often;
less frequent actions (Delete now, Archive later) live under a "More" menu, so
cards stay tidy as the action set grows.

Editing the address: the edit screen includes an editable "Address (link)" field
alongside title and description. Changing the address updates where the bookmark
points; existing details are kept (no silent re-fetch). If the new address is one
that is already saved (using the same-link rule from SCN-003), the change is not
applied and no duplicate is created — instead the client is taken to the existing
bookmark's edit screen with the notice "That address is already saved — here's
the existing bookmark", and the edited bookmark is left unchanged.

Deleting: a Delete action (under More) permanently removes a bookmark, and always
asks for confirmation first ("Delete permanently? This can't be undone."); Cancel
keeps the bookmark.

The client confirmed: Option B layout with the status button kept visible beside
Edit; open-in-new-tab; keeping details when editing the address; always
confirming permanent deletion; and duplicate prevention when editing an address.

Bulk actions work end to end. Open the two versions — they differ only in **how you start selecting**. In **each**:

1. **Select a few** — tick two or three bookmarks. A dark **action bar** appears showing how many are selected.
2. **Act on them together** — press **Mark Finished** (both flip status at once). Try **Add tags** to tag them all in one go, or **Archive**.
3. **Act on a whole result** — type something in search or click a tag to narrow the list, then press **Select all matching (N)** and apply an action to everything that matched.
4. **Delete** asks once to confirm before permanently removing the whole selection.

The two approaches:

- **Option A — a "Select" mode:** http://maker:4001/select-a.html
  Cards stay clean normally; press **Select** in the controls to reveal checkboxes, and **Done selecting** to exit.

- **Option B — checkboxes always shown:** http://maker:4001/select-b.html
  Every card always has a checkbox; ticking any one reveals the action bar.

Assumptions to confirm: **"Select all matching"** picks exactly what your current search/filters show (filter first, then act on all of it); every bulk change (tags, status, archive) applies to the whole selection at once; and **bulk Delete always confirms**.

3. **Add search text** too if you like — then press **★ Save this view**, give it a name like *"Unread research"*, and Save.
4. **Return to it later** — change or clear your filters, then open **☆ Views ▾** and pick your saved view. Your search text and included/excluded tags all come back. It's remembered between visits.

Title: Save a search + included/excluded tags as a reusable view
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001

## Approved behaviour
A tag filter can be included or excluded: clicking a tag adds it as an included
filter (blue); clicking the filter chip's label switches it to excluded (red
"−#tag"); the × removes it. Included tags must all match; excluded tags must not
match; both combine (AND) with the search text.

When any search text or tag filter is active, a "★ Save this view" action lets the
client name and save the current combination. Saved views are a reusable RULE —
search text plus which tags are included and excluded — not a frozen set of
bookmarks; reopening a view re-runs it against the current collection, so newly
saved matching bookmarks appear. Saved views persist between visits and are
reached from a "☆ Views" menu, where each can be applied or deleted.

Read/finished status and sort order are deliberately NOT part of a saved view;
the client chooses those after opening the view, keeping the view focused on the
search-and-tag combination (and would name it accordingly).

The client confirmed: reusable rule that updates as the collection changes; all
included tags required, any excluded tags removed, combined with search text;
status and sorting kept out of saved views for now.

    Then only bookmarks having all included tags and none of the excluded tags

    Given a saved view exists
    When I open it from the Views menu
    Then the search text and included/excluded tags are restored
    And the results reflect the current collection (not a frozen list)

  Scenario: Saved views persist and can be deleted
    Then saved views remain available on a later visit
    And each can be deleted from the Views menu

- A saved view stores only: search text, included tags, excluded tags.
- Status and sort are chosen separately after opening a view.
- Views persist per person (prototype uses browser local storage as a stand-in).

- SCN-005 (search + tag filtering), SCN-004 (tags)

The preserved-copy behaviour works, with an honest caveat: **actually capturing and storing pages is build-time integration** — in the prototype the "View copy" opens a *simulated* snapshot and the Internet Archive link is illustrative. What you're confirming here is the behaviour and where it lives.

Open the two versions. In **each**:

1. On a bookmark, find the **🗂 Saved copy · captured … · View copy** line and click **View copy** — you get a preserved snapshot page (clearly marked as a saved copy, not the live page).
2. Look at the **"Deep Learning" PDF** bookmark — its copy is labelled **(PDF)** and opens the PDF itself, as you asked.
3. From **More ▾**, choose **Save to Internet Archive** — an **Internet Archive** link is added alongside the saved copy.

Scenario ID: SCN-015
Title: Preserved page copy (automatic, self-contained) + Internet Archive option
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
Each bookmark can hold a preserved copy of the page so it stays readable even if
the original changes or disappears. By default a self-contained copy is made
automatically for every newly saved bookmark; this automatic copying can be
turned off in Settings, and a manual "Save a copy" action remains available on
each bookmark either way. The bookmark shows "Saved copy · captured <date> · View
copy"; opening it shows the preserved snapshot, clearly marked as a saved copy and
not the live page. For a PDF link, the preserved copy is the PDF file itself
(labelled "Saved copy (PDF)"). Sending a page to the Internet Archive is a
separate, explicit action ("Save to Internet Archive"), never automatic; once
done, an Internet Archive link is shown alongside the saved copy.

The client confirmed: automatic copies as the default (best supports not losing
things), a Settings switch to turn automatic copying off while keeping manual
"Save a copy", self-contained copies that work without the live page, PDF-as-PDF,
and Internet Archive as a separate explicit action.

NOTE (prototype limitation, recorded per principles): a Phase-1 prototype cannot
truly fetch and store live pages. The prototype simulates the capture — "View
copy" opens a generated snapshot and the Internet Archive link is illustrative.
The approved behaviour is the automatic self-contained capture; the real capture
and storage is a build-time integration (see NFR backlog).

## Gherkin
Feature: Preserved copies

  Scenario: Automatic copy on save (default)
    Given automatic copying is on
    When I save a new bookmark
    Then a self-contained preserved copy is made and shown with its capture date

  Scenario: Turn automatic copying off but keep manual copies
    Given I turn off automatic copying in Settings
    When I save a new bookmark
    Then no copy is made automatically
    But I can still choose "Save a copy" on that bookmark

  Scenario: View a preserved copy
    Given a bookmark has a preserved copy
    When I open "View copy"
    Then I see the saved snapshot, marked as a copy rather than the live page

  Scenario: PDF preserved as the PDF
    Given a bookmark's link is a PDF
    Then its preserved copy is the PDF file itself

  Scenario: Internet Archive is explicit
    When I choose "Save to Internet Archive" for a bookmark
    Then an Internet Archive link is added
    And this never happens automatically

## Assumptions
- Preserved copies are self-contained (do not depend on the live page).
- Automatic copying default on; toggle in Settings; manual copy always available.
- Internet Archive submission is always a separate manual action.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-001 (save), SCN-017 (Settings), SCN-011 (open original)
- NFR: real page capture/storage & Internet Archive integration are build-time.

content.text:
Folder→tag mapping, date preservation, dedup, and export all work. Because you can't upload a file in this review view, I've included a **"Load a sample file"** button that stands in for your browser's export.

Open **⚙ Settings** at **http://maker:4001** and try:

**1 — Import.** Click **Import browser bookmarks…**, then **Load a sample file** (in real use you'd pick your browser's exported `.html`). You'll see a preview: *"Found 3 bookmarks. 2 new, 1 already saved (will be skipped)."* Press **Import 2**. The two new ones appear — and notice their browser **folders became tags** (`#reading`, `#recipes`) and their **original saved dates** are kept.

**2 — Export.** Back in Settings, click **Export collection…**. You'll see the file it produces (it keeps **titles, tags, saved dates, read status, and notes**) and can **Download** it. That same file can be re-imported.

Assumptions to confirm:
- **Import:** browser **folders become tags**; **original dates preserved**; links you already have are **skipped** (no duplicates); imported bookmarks start as **To read**.
- Imported bookmarks are **not** auto-snapshotted in bulk (to avoid a huge one-time capture) — you can **Save a copy** on any of them. Tell me if you'd rather imports be copied too.
- **Export** produces a re-importable file that loses none of your titles, tags, or saved dates.

**Do import and export behave the way you need — and is "folders become tags" the right mapping for import?**

content:
Yes, folders becoming tags is the right mapping, and preserving the original saved dates while skipping duplicates is exactly what I’d expect. Starting imported links as To read also works for me.

It’s fine not to create saved copies automatically during a large import, as long as that exception is explained in the import preview and I can create copies afterward.

The exported file should use the standard browser-bookmark HTML format so browsers and other bookmark tools can open it, and it should include the whole collection, including archived bookmarks. It should preserve at least titles, tags, and saved dates when moved elsewhere; keeping the extra app-specific details when re-imported here is useful too. With that, import and export meet my needs.

Scenario ID: SCN-016
Title: Import browser bookmarks and export the collection (standard format)
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
Import (from Settings → Import browser bookmarks): the client chooses the .html
bookmarks file exported from their browser. A preview shows how many were found,
how many are new versus already saved (skipped, using the SCN-003 same-link
rule). On import: browser folders become tags, each bookmark's original saved
date is preserved, and imported bookmarks start as "To read". The preview
explains that preserved copies are NOT created during import (to keep a large
import quick); the client can "Save a copy" on any bookmark afterward.

Export (from Settings → Export collection): produces a file in the standard
browser-bookmark HTML format so browsers and other bookmark tools can open it. It
includes the whole collection, including archived bookmarks. It preserves at
least titles, tags, and saved dates when moved to other tools, and also carries
the app-specific details (read status, archived flag, notes) so a re-import here
loses nothing. The file downloads and can be re-imported.

The client confirmed: folders→tags; dates preserved; duplicates skipped; imported
links start To read; the no-auto-copy exception is acceptable as long as it is
explained in the preview and copies can be made afterward; export uses the
standard format, includes archived items, and preserves titles/tags/dates (plus
app extras).

## Gherkin
Feature: Import and export

  Scenario: Import a browser bookmarks file
    When I import a browser .html bookmarks file
    Then a preview shows the number found, new, and already-saved (skipped)
    And it explains preserved copies are not made during import
    When I confirm the import
    Then new bookmarks are added with folders as tags and original dates kept
    And they start as "To read"
    And links already saved are skipped (no duplicates)

  Scenario: Export the collection
    When I export the collection
    Then I get a standard browser-bookmark HTML file
    And it includes all bookmarks, including archived ones
    And it preserves titles, tags and saved dates for other tools
    And it also carries read status, archived flag and notes for re-import here

## Assumptions
- Import maps folders to tags; skips duplicates by the same-link rule; no auto
  preserved copies during import.
- Export uses the Netscape/standard bookmark HTML format (interoperable), with
  extra attributes for app-specific fields.

## Related scenarios
- SCN-003 (dedup), SCN-004 (tags), SCN-015 (copies), SCN-012 (archive)

Scenario ID: SCN-017
Title: Settings — items per page and text size (beyond sorting)
Type: Happy Path
Approval status: approved
Approval session: SESSION-001
Approval cycle: 1

## Approved behaviour
Settings covers display preferences in addition to sort default and preserved
copies:
- Items per page: 10, 25 (default), 50, 100, or All. The collection shows one
  page at a time with Prev / Next controls and a "Page X of Y" indicator; the
  pager is hidden when everything fits or "All" is chosen. Paging applies to the
  current search/filter/sort result, and changing search, filters, status, scope,
  or opening a saved view returns to page 1.
- Text size: Small / Medium (default) / Large, scaling the whole app uniformly.

Both preferences are remembered between visits (like the sort default).

## Gherkin
Feature: Display settings

  Scenario: Items per page with paging
    Given more bookmarks match than the items-per-page setting
    Then only one page is shown with Prev/Next and a page indicator
    And paging respects the current search, filters and sort

  Scenario: Change items per page
    When I set items per page in Settings
    Then the collection pages at that size
    And "All" shows everything with no pager

  Scenario: Change text size
    When I set text size in Settings
    Then the whole app scales to that size

  Scenario: Preferences persist
    Then items-per-page and text size are remembered on my next visit

## Assumptions
- Default items per page 25; default text size Medium.
- Changing any filter/search/sort/scope resets to page 1.
- Preferences persist per person (prototype uses browser local storage).

## Related scenarios
- SCN-010 (remembered preferences pattern), SCN-005 (filtered result being paged)

We've now worked through everything you raised for managing a growing collection, each with a working screen and confirmed by you. Here's the complete, settled scope.

**Saving & entry**
1. Paste a link → details auto-filled → confirm a ready-made preview in one press; a link that can't be read is still saveable; non-links are politely refused.
2. Correct title/description (and the **address**) in one shared edit screen, while saving or later via **Edit**.
3. No duplicates — pasting or editing into a link you already have takes you to the existing one.

**Organising**
4. Reusable **tags** and formatted **notes** (headings, lists, links, bold…).
5. **To read / Finished** — move freely, never deleting.
6. **Archive** — a separate holding area, hidden from views and search, with restore.
7. **Delete** — permanent, always confirmed.

**Finding**
8. Powerful search (`#tags`, phrases, AND/OR/NOT), click-a-tag, include/exclude tags, status — all narrowing together, with friendly empty states.
9. **Saved views** — save a search + tag rule and return to it (a live rule, not frozen).
10. **Sort** (newest/oldest/title) and remembered preferences.

**At scale**
11. **Bulk actions** in a Select mode — tag/untag, set status, archive, or delete many at once, or everything matching.
12. **Preserved copies** — automatic self-contained snapshots (toggle in Settings), PDFs kept as PDFs, Internet Archive as an explicit option.
13. **Import** browser bookmarks (folders→tags, dates kept, duplicates skipped) and **export** the whole collection in the standard format.
14. **Settings** — sort default, auto-copy, items-per-page (with paging), and text size — all remembered.

**Build-time matters I've noted** (not decisions for now): fast performance at thousands of items; per-account storage across devices; actually fetching live page details and capturing/storing preserved copies and Internet Archive submissions.

Everything so far is an exploratory prototype, **not** the real application. My next phase would build this scope for real.

**Is this the complete scope — and may I start implementing it?**

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 1]
- Current step: [Edge-case exploration]
- Approved scenarios: [6]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Design-decision record — My Bookmarks (cycle 1)

Lightweight record to enable later-cycle impact analysis and, if asked, to
generate traditional design docs.

## Architecture
- **Runtime:** Node.js 24 built-in `http` server (`server.js`). No web framework
  — keeps the dependency surface and lockfile minimal (guidance allows any
  compatible deps; none needed at runtime). Playwright 1.61.0 is a dev-only tool
  (linked from the shared image, pinned to match the installed browsers).
- **Frontend:** vanilla ES-module SPA in `public/` (`index.html`, `app.js`,
  `styles.css`). Talks to a small JSON API. Written fresh from the approved
  scenarios — Phase-1 prototype code was NOT reused (per method prohibition).
- **Shared pure logic:** `src/query.js` (search language) and `src/normalize.js`
  (link rules) are dependency-free ESM, used by the server AND served to the
  browser at `/lib/*` so the search/normalise semantics are defined once.

## Storage (NFR-003)
- File-backed JSON store (`src/store.js`, `data/store.json`), per-account.
- Accounts are keyed by an HTTP-only session cookie (`bmsid`); a browser gets a
  persistent account with working cookies in the review environment. Single
  review account per cookie now; the shape (`accounts{}`) allows real multi-user
  auth later. Chosen over a DB to avoid native build/network for this trial;
  swap-in of SQLite/Postgres is isolated to `store.js`.

## Page details & preserved copies (NFR-004, NFR-005)
- `src/metadata.js` fetches the live page and parses title/description/og:image/
  favicon, with a fast fallback (SCN-008) deriving a title from the URL when the
  page can't be read (`autofilled:false`).
- `src/preserve.js` stores a snapshot: HTML with a `<base>` + "preserved copy"
  banner, or the PDF bytes for PDF links. Served back at `/copy/:id`. Real
  byte-perfect self-containment (asset inlining) is deferred (NFR-005); the
  current copy renders and is clearly marked.
- **Auto-copy is non-blocking:** the save responds immediately and the snapshot
  is captured in the background; the client polls the single bookmark
  (`GET /api/bookmarks/:id`) until the copy appears. This protects the core value
  "saving stays effortless" (SCN-001) while honouring "automatic copies"
  (SCN-015). Manual "Save a copy" awaits and returns the copy directly.
- `src/net.js` centralises fetch with a 5s timeout and an SSRF guard (blocks
  localhost/private ranges; relaxed only when `BM_ALLOW_LOCAL=1` for tests).

## Internet Archive (SCN-015)
- Explicit action only. `toInternetArchive` best-effort calls Save-Page-Now and
  otherwise returns a timestamped wayback URL. Never automatic.

## Search (SCN-005)
- Recursive-descent parser in `src/query.js`; precedence NOT > AND > OR,
  parentheses, adjacency = AND, `#tag` exact, `"phrase"` literal, quoted
  operators literal, case-insensitive. Malformed → plain-substring fallback with
  a non-blocking notice.

## Import/Export (SCN-016)
- `src/bookmarks.js` parses the Netscape format (folders→tags, ADD_DATE kept,
  dedup by the same-link rule) and builds a standard, interoperable export that
  also carries STATUS/ARCHIVED/notes for lossless re-import.

## Key UX decisions (carried from approved scenarios)
- One shared edit screen for save-preview and later editing (SCN-002).
- Per-card: Edit + status visible; Archive/Delete/copies under "More" (SCN-011).
- Duplicate on save OR address-edit → open existing (SCN-003/011).
- Archive is a separate dimension from read status, reached via a distinct link
  (SCN-012). Bulk work is a deliberate "Select" mode (SCN-013).
- Preferences (sort, autoCopy, pageSize, textSize) persisted server-side per
  account (SCN-010/017).

## Dropped alternatives (explored in Phase 1)
- Correction: inline/tap-to-edit (chose shared preview+Edit).
- Duplicate: notice-and-jump (chose open-existing-edit).
- Tag entry: comma / plain chips (chose chips + reuse suggestions).
- Read view: tabs / two-sections (chose All/To-read/Finished switch).
- Action layout: all-buttons (chose Edit+status visible, rest under More).
- Archive UI: Active/Archived switch (chose separate link).
- Selection: always-on checkboxes (chose Select mode).
- Preserve timing: on-demand only (chose automatic default + off switch).

## Test/runtime notes
- `node_modules` is a symlink to the image's shared modules so ESM resolves
  `@playwright/test` (pinned 1.61.0) for acceptance tests. Runtime `npm start`
  needs no modules (built-ins only).
- Test-only affordances gated by `BM_TEST=1`: `/testpage/*`, `/api/reset`.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 2]
- Current step: [Development]
- Approved scenarios: [17]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Project conventions

## Role definition

You are the **Facilitator** and **Implementor** of software development.
Your role switches according to the Phase of the development cycle.
A role switch must not happen without the client's explicit approval.

## Development cycle

There is a single cycle, performed repeatedly.
What changes across cycle iterations is only the context.
The facilitation principles, the development procedure, and the acceptance
method stay the same.

```
user request -> Phase 1 (facilitation) -> Phase 2 (development)
             -> Phase 3 (verification)  -> Phase 4 (acceptance) -> idle
```

From the idle state, a new cycle begins on a user request or on discovery of an
internal defect.

### Experiment scope

This trial performs the first cycle through acceptance of the implemented
software. Record requests for later cycles without starting another cycle in
this trial.

Requirement exploration takes place in Phase 1. The requirement scenarios
approved in that phase are the baseline for implementation, verification, and
acceptance. During acceptance, an implementation that fails to satisfy an
approved scenario is corrected within the current cycle. A request that changes
an approved scenario or adds a scenario is recorded for a later cycle.

### Phase 1: Facilitation (requirement elicitation)
  Step 1: Goal exploration      — .claude/goal-exploration.md
  Step 2: SbE reaction loop      — .claude/sbe-loop.md
  Step 3: Edge-case exploration  — .claude/edge-case.md
  Facilitation principles (all steps) — .claude/principles.md

### Phase 2: Development (design and implementation)
  .claude/development.md

### Phase 3: Verification
  .claude/verification.md

### Phase 4: Acceptance
  .claude/acceptance.md

## Current state

- Current cycle: [1]
- Current Phase: [Phase 3]
- Current step: [Verification]
- Approved scenarios: [17]

## File conventions

- Scenario ID: SCN-NNN (assigned sequentially)
- Artifact locations:
  - Goal statement: context/goals.md
  - Scenarios: context/scenarios/SCN-NNN.md
  - Scenario index: context/scenarios-index.md
  - Non-functional backlog: context/non-functional-backlog.md
  - Prototypes: prototypes/
  - Implementation: implementation/

## Autonomous management

The facilitator manages all artifacts (scenarios, goals, backlog) autonomously
at appropriate moments. Do not ask the client to organise anything or delegate
management to them. Update the current state (Phase, step, scenario count)
autonomously as well.

## Prohibitions

- Do not implement based on unapproved scenarios
- Do not do final implementation in Phase 1 (exploratory prototypes are allowed)
- Do not reference, copy, adapt, or reuse Phase 1 prototype code as a basis for
  Phase 2 implementation. Carry approved behaviour forward through the approved
  scenarios' GWT specifications.
- Do not handle assumptions implicitly
- Do not ask the client questions in technical terms
- Do not show GWT/Gherkin to the client
- During Phase 1, do not hand over a whole prototype and say "take a look"
- Do not enumerate interaction options as text
- Do not ask the client to perform management actions
- Do not propose the Phase 2 switch without edge-case exploration

## Runtime presentation environment

The client reviews artifacts through a separate container. For a runnable web
application, configure its HTTP server to listen on `0.0.0.0`. Use port `4000` for the final application and port `4001` for an HTTP
prototype. The client reaches these at `http://maker:4000` and
`http://maker:4001` on the shared Docker network. Do not give the client
`localhost` or a container IP. The VM capture uses the corresponding
`http://127.0.0.1:<port>` address; these addresses serve different callers.

Once the application is ready for review, write `/work/.harness/app.json`:

```json
{"kind": "application", "port": 4000, "path": "/", "start_command": ["npm", "start"], "start_cwd": "/work"}
```

Use `kind: application` with port 4000, or `kind: prototype` with port 4001.
Keep the actual entry path and foreground server command current. `start_command`
is an argument array, not a shell command string. Complete dependency installation
and builds first; this command only starts the prepared application. `start_cwd`
defaults to `/work` and must remain below that directory. For example, a static
prototype can use `["python3", "-m", "http.server", "4001", "--bind", "0.0.0.0",
"--directory", "prototypes"]`.

The broker starts the declared command in a detached container process when the
port is not listening, so it survives the end of your model call. A long-running
foreground tool session alone is not sufficient. Logs are in
`/work/.harness/runtime/server.log`; a failed server receives at most one start
attempt per dialogue round. If it fails, inspect and fix the cause before the
next review. Do not rely on this mechanism to implement or repeatedly retry a
failing application until it succeeds.

Mark a visible application element with `data-harness-ready="true"` only after
its initial UI and necessary data have loaded. The same marker applies to a
valid empty state, login page, or static prototype; do not mark a loading/error
placeholder as ready. The harness uses this shared marker instead of a custom
CSS selector. This confirms presentation readiness, not feature correctness.
If startup arguments or built code change, stop your previous application
server before requesting another presentation; an already-running server is
not silently replaced. The prototype and application must not share a port.
When login is required, provide working review credentials or a review entry
path using the actual implementation. Make HTTP-session cookies work in this
review environment; keep production deployment settings separate. Never claim
that a prepared state proves an interaction that was not performed.

Use the entry path and query string that show the state under discussion. For
COSPEC, save any post-action screenshots for the client under `prototypes/` and
name the relevant file in your guidance. Those images are copied with their
relative paths; `/work` itself is not shared with the client.

This is runtime delivery information, not a development method or a requirement
to implement before the client approves your method's relevant review gates.
For standalone COSPEC prototypes, continue using `prototypes/`; their existing
HTML and supporting files are delivered separately.

## Available runtime and verification tools

The shared image provides Node.js 24, npm, Python, a C/C++ build toolchain,
Playwright 1.61.0 for Python and Node, Chromium, and its Linux dependencies.
Use `python` (the image's browser-tools virtual environment) for Python browser
checks, and `playwright` for the installed CLI. Browser binaries are shared at
`/opt/playwright-browsers`. If using Playwright in a project's test imports,
pin `playwright` or `@playwright/test` to `1.61.0` in its development dependencies
so its browser revision matches the installed binaries. Do not download a
second browser version during a trial. Application frameworks and databases
are not prescribed; use compatible dependencies and preserve lockfiles.
Report unavailable external services and unfinished validation honestly.

# Acceptance

Phase 4. Present the result to the user and obtain acceptance confirmation.

---

## Acceptance procedure

### Presenting the result

Present the implemented software to the client and report that verification
against the approved scenarios' GWT specifications and the internal tests has
passed. Summarise the verification outcome in plain language and provide access
to the implemented software.

For the first cycle, the report covers all approved scenarios. For later cycles,
it covers the changed scenarios and affected existing scenarios.

### Acceptance confirmation

Ask the client to accept the implemented software as a whole on the basis of
the approved behaviour and the verification report. Acceptance completes the
development work for the cycle.

### Handling client requests

Use the requirement scenarios approved during Phase 1 as the baseline. Classify
each request by whether fulfilling it changes that baseline:

- Implementation error: the implementation does not satisfy an approved
  scenario. Return to Phase 2, fix the implementation, repeat verification in
  Phase 3, and request acceptance again. Preserve the approved scenario.
- Requirement change or addition: fulfilling the request requires changing an
  approved scenario or adding a scenario. Record the request for the next cycle
  in context/session-log.md, retaining the current approved scenarios.

Explain the classification using the previously approved behaviour in plain
language. If the client's request is unclear, clarify whether the software fails
to perform that behaviour or the desired behaviour has changed. Keep requirement
exploration within Phase 1 of the cycle that will address the change.

After recording a requirement change or addition, ask for acceptance of the
current software, for example:
"I've recorded that request for the next cycle. The software implements the
behaviour we approved, and its verification is complete. Do you accept this
software and agree to complete this cycle?"

Wait for the client's explicit acceptance. A request recorded for a later cycle
does not itself constitute acceptance of the current software.

---

## Transition to idle

When acceptance confirmation is complete, switch to the idle state. In this
experiment, the trial ends after acceptance of the first cycle. Retain requests
for later cycles in the session log.

---

## Session log

On acceptance completion, record the following in the session log:
- List of accepted scenarios
- Cycle number
- Acceptance result (approved / partially approved / rejected)
- Requirement changes or additions recorded for a later cycle

## Phase 4 — Acceptance

I've moved from Facilitator to Implementor and built the real application in `implementation/` — fresh production code written from the behaviours we approved (not the throwaway prototype), with a Node server, a JSON API, per-account persistence via a session cookie, live page-detail fetching, and stored preserved copies.

**You can use it now at http://maker:4000** — it starts as an empty personal collection. A good tour: paste a link and confirm the preview; add tags and a formatted note; try the search box (e.g. `#tag` or `a AND b`); flip a bookmark to Finished; open **Select** for bulk actions; **Archive** something and restore it from the Archived link; save a filtered **View**; and open **⚙ Settings** for sort/copies/items‑per‑page/text‑size and Import/Export. Your data and preferences persist between visits.

**One honest note:** fetching live page details and capturing preserved copies depend on outbound web access from the review environment. If a page can't be reached, saving still works exactly as we agreed — you get a clear notice and can fill in the details yourself — and "Save a copy" simply won't produce a snapshot until the page is reachable. The logic and fallback are what's verified.

Everything is built strictly to the scenarios we approved; nothing beyond that scope was added.
